title: Nehemiah 4:1–6
context: Sanballat and Tobiah mock the Jews’ rebuilding, ridiculing their strength and their wall. Nehemiah answers with a prayer committing the insult to God, and the people keep building until the wall reaches half its height, “for the people had a mind to work.” Versification: English 4:1–6 is Hebrew 3:33–38, and English 4:7–23 is Hebrew 4:1–17; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about prayer, perseverance, and entrusting judgment to God.

verses.text: But when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry, and was very indignant, and mocked the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Sanballat hears that the wall is being built, he is angry and indignant and mocks the Jews. Opposition intensifies.

Arminian readers see hostile human choices set against the work of God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sanballat the Horonite has opposed Nehemiah since 2:10 and 2:19. His motives are not fully stated, though political interests are often suggested.

Reformed readers see opposition as a recurring feature of God’s work. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He spoke before his brothers and the army of Samaria, and said, “What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they fortify themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, since they are burned?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Before his associates and the army of Samaria, Sanballat ridicules the feeble Jews, asking whether they will fortify, sacrifice, finish in a day, or revive burned stones from the rubble. Mockery aims to discourage.

Arminian readers see words used as weapons.
verses.reformedNotes:
The questions mock both the builders’ strength and their hopes. The presence of an army adds a note of menace.

Reformed readers see the world despising what God is doing. Both traditions read this as shared ground about enduring ridicule.

verses.text: Now Tobiah the Ammonite was by him, and he said, “What they are building, if a fox climbed up it, he would break down their stone wall.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Tobiah the Ammonite adds that if a fox climbed their wall, it would break it down. The scorn is sharpened.

Arminian readers see contempt meant to persuade the builders that their labor is worthless.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tobiah has been linked with Sanballat since 2:10. The jibe is rhetorical, and the narrative will show it to be empty.

Reformed readers see God’s work often appearing weak in the eyes of opponents. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithfulness in the face of contempt.

verses.text: “Hear, our God, for we are despised. Turn back their reproach on their own head. Give them up for a plunder in a land of captivity.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah prays that God will hear, because they are despised, and turn their reproach back on the mockers. He brings the insult to God.

Arminian readers see an appeal to God’s justice instead of personal retaliation.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prayer resembles imprecatory prayers in the Psalms; how such prayers are read is treated in the boxes at Psalm 35:4 and Psalm 109:6.

Reformed readers likewise see the cause committed to God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about entrusting judgment to God.

verses.text: Don’t cover their iniquity. Don’t let their sin be blotted out from before you; for they have insulted the builders.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah asks God not to cover their iniquity or blot out their sin, for they have insulted the builders. The prayer is severe.

Arminian readers see opposition to God’s work treated as a serious offense against God himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
The words are an appeal for judgment, not an act of vengeance; Nehemiah leaves the matter with God and returns to work.

Reformed readers see God as the defender of his people. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground, without adding a new box.

verses.text: So we built the wall; and all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.
verses.arminianNotes:
So they build, and the whole wall is joined to half its height, for the people have a mind to work. Prayer is followed by labor.

Arminian readers see a people freely and wholeheartedly committed to the task.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘a mind to work’ credits the people’s resolve. Progress continues despite mockery.

Reformed readers see God strengthening his people’s hearts for the work. Both traditions read this as shared ground about prayer and diligent labor going together, without setting one against the other.
